name: Radiomics
title: Radiomics
answer: Radiomics is the extraction of quantitative features from medical images, such as CT, MRI, and PET scans, to build models that support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response assessment. It sits within diagnostic imaging and radiology, and it turns images into numerical data that can be analyzed alongside clinical and genomic information. The features describe shape, intensity, and texture, and they are often grouped into first-order, shape, and texture families. Radiomics is distinct from deep learning that learns features directly from pixels, though the two approaches increasingly overlap in practice. It applies across oncology, neurology, and other specialties where imaging is central to care.

sections.body: Radiomics is the extraction of quantitative features from medical images, such as CT, MRI, and PET scans, to build models that support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response assessment. It sits within diagnostic imaging and radiology, and it turns images into numerical data that can be analyzed alongside clinical and genomic information. The features describe shape, intensity, and texture, and they are often grouped into first-order, shape, and texture families. Radiomics is distinct from deep learning that learns features directly from pixels, though the two approaches increasingly overlap in practice. It applies across oncology, neurology, and other specialties where imaging is central to care.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Radiomics runs on standard imaging data from CT, MRI, and PET scanners, usually retrieved from a PACS in DICOM format. The work is done on workstations or compute clusters, and it relies on software libraries such as PyRadiomics for feature extraction. Segmentation of the region of interest is a key input, and it can be manual, semi-automated, or fully automated. The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative, or IBSI, provides a reference for consistent feature definitions across tools. De-identification and secure storage are part of the infrastructure because images and derived features are sensitive data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The workflow begins with image acquisition and segmentation of the target region, followed by feature extraction using a standardized library. Feature selection then reduces hundreds or thousands of candidate features to a smaller set that is stable and relevant. A machine learning model, such as a random forest or support vector machine, is trained on those features, often with cross-validation and external validation. Reproducibility depends on documenting acquisition parameters, segmentation method, and software version, and on following reporting guidelines like the Radiomics Quality Score. The result is a pipeline that can be audited, not a single opaque model.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Radiomics uses medical images and derived data, so privacy rules such as HIPAA and GDPR apply, and secondary use typically requires de-identification and sometimes consent. Provenance matters because a model's output depends on the scanner, acquisition protocol, segmentation, and feature extraction version, all of which should be recorded. Regulatory status varies, with some radiomics tools cleared as medical devices and many remaining research use only. Risk includes overfitting, poor generalization across sites, and bias from unrepresentative training data, and the site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies as a reminder that liability is live. Intellectual property can be complex when algorithms are proprietary or built on open-source components.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Radiomics is moving toward tighter integration with deep learning, often called deep radiomics, and toward multimodal models that combine imaging with genomics and clinical data. Standardization efforts like IBSI and prospective clinical trials are pushing the field from retrospective research toward clinical decision support. Regulatory frameworks are maturing, and the site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, which reflects the growing attention to validation and post-market surveillance. Challenges remain in generalization across scanners and populations, and in making the outputs explainable to radiologists. The likely path is not replacement of the radiologist but augmentation of reading workflows with quantitative evidence.
